name: Grace Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Grace, thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a two-boom jumbo drill underground at a gold mine, about nine hundred metres down, and I lead the development crew on day shift. We drill the face, a pattern of about sixty holes, so the charge-up crew can blast and we push the tunnel forward another four metres. Start is half five, ride the cage down, gas check, scale the back, then I'm on the drill most of the day. I like that you can measure your work: four metres yesterday, four metres today.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The heat at the bottom levels, and the noise, even with plugs in. Also being the only woman on the crew who's a lead, so every mistake I make gets remembered longer. But my crew's good now. Marek, our shotfirer, eats lunch with me on an upturned bucket and tells me about his allotment, and that's the best twenty minutes of the day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So, more of the same. I can picture that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now can we talk about the ventilation fans instead. That's what actually needs fixing on our level. Online I'd probably share some article about the AI bubble with a little eye-roll.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a bit disappointed and a bit relieved. Some of the AI tools are handy, I use one now and then to tidy up my shift reports so they don't sound like I wrote them on my knee. But I'd rather keep my drill than have something brilliant replace it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. I'd finish the leading hand course the company's offering next spring, and keep putting a bit aside each pay, I've got about three months of rent and bills. Maybe start sending my mum a bit more each month, since nothing's shaking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a normal Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said teleremote drilling is a thing already. Does it come up in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, a bit. Our sister mine trialled a jumbo you run from the surface, and it took them eighteen months to get it working because the network kept dropping. So in this picture I'd guess they try it here too and it's slow. I'd watch, I wouldn't volunteer first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not volunteer first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the first crew does all the swearing and fixing and gets none of the credit. I'd rather go second, once the bugs are out. That's not fear, it's just how I work, same as I didn't buy a phone until my sister had one for a year.

S0.say: Good, now can we talk about the ventilation fans on our level instead. I'd share an article about the AI bubble online with a bit of an eye-roll.
S0.think: I'd be a bit disappointed and a bit relieved. I use AI now and then to tidy up shift reports, but I'd rather keep my drill than have something brilliant replace it.
S0.do: Finishes the company's leading hand course next spring and keeps saving, at about three months of bills. Sends her mum a bit more each month and watches the teleremote drill trial without volunteering first.
S0.quote: The first crew does all the swearing and fixing and gets none of the credit.
S0.fieldNote: Grace is precise and measures her life in metres of tunnel. She's open to new tech but prefers to go second, once others have proven it, and is clear that this is method rather than fear. Her money is fairly tight because she sends some home to her mother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, this one I'd believe more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the union needs to be at the table before the first remote drill goes in, not after. And I'd say it at work loudly enough that the shift boss hears. Online I'd share the union's posts and argue with my cousin in the comments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What it really means is the drill goes to the surface and maybe I go with it. Surface work's not bad, it's cooler and there's daylight. But they won't need one operator per drill up there, they'll have one person watching three, so two of us are spare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until the first teleremote crew had six months on it, then put my hand up for the training. Meanwhile I'd keep saving and try to push my cushion from three to five months over the year. I'd get onto the union's safety committee, because remote systems change who's responsible when something goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep, but I'd start counting who on the crew would make the cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you count first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marek, honestly. He's fifty-one, brilliant with explosives, and he can barely work the canteen card machine. I'd worry about him more than me. I'd probably sit with him and go through the training stuff on my phone at lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said one person watching three drills. What happens to the other two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit nobody at head office says out loud. The good answer is they move into maintenance or into new parts of the mine. The likely answer is they don't replace people who retire and call it natural attrition. I'd want that written down in the agreement, not just promised in a toolbox talk.

S1.say: The union needs to be at the table before the first remote drill goes in, not after. I'd say it loudly enough at work for the shift boss to hear.
S1.think: The drill goes to the surface and maybe I go with it, which isn't bad. But they'll have one person watching three drills, so two of us are spare.
S1.do: Waits six months for the first teleremote crew to prove the system, then volunteers for training. Builds her savings from three to five months over the year and joins the union safety committee.
S1.feel: Uneasy, starting to count who on the crew would make the cut.
S1.quote: They won't need one operator per drill up there, they'll have one person watching three, so two of us are spare.
S1.fieldNote: Grace quickly does the maths on staffing: remote work means fewer operators, not just different ones. Her worry turns quickly to older colleagues like Marek. She wants protections in writing, which fits both her progressive views and her careful, step-by-step style.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's, wow. That's before my next pay rise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly what governments are for, and they'd better move faster than they did with anything else. At work I'd be calm, because people look at the lead hand. Online I'd say we need a public wage floor, not handouts from companies when they feel like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be scared. My whole plan was go second, let the others test it. With two years there's no second. Everyone goes at once and the robots don't need a lead hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month I'd cut what I can: the gym, takeaway, the trip to my sister's wedding abroad would turn into a video call, which would break my heart. I'd keep sending Mum money as long as I could. I'd go to every union and community meeting, and I'd write to my local member for the first time in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like when the gas monitor goes off and you don't know yet if it's real or a faulty sensor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning buy you, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe enough time to stop spending and get to six months saved. Not enough time to retrain, because what would I retrain into? I'd be learning something that's gone by the time I finish the course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stay calm at work. Is that true?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On the outside, yes. Inside I'd be checking the job boards in the toilet at break. I think a lead hand who panics just makes everyone else panic. So I'd fake it, and then cry in the car, probably.

S2.say: This is what governments are for, and they need to move faster than ever. We need a public wage floor, not handouts from companies when they feel like it.
S2.think: I'd be scared, because my whole plan was to go second and let others test it. With two years there's no second, everyone goes at once and robots don't need a lead hand.
S2.do: Cuts the gym and takeaways, and swaps the trip to her sister's wedding abroad for a video call. Keeps sending money to her mum, attends every union and community meeting, and writes to her local member for the first time.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like a gas monitor going off before you know if it's real. Calm on the outside at work, crying in the car after.
S2.quote: My whole plan was go second, let the others test it. With two years there's no second.
S2.fieldNote: The speed of this scenario breaks Grace's main coping strategy, waiting for others to go first. She'd keep a calm face for her crew and hide the fear. Missing her sister's wedding was the detail that seemed to hurt her most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, I can breathe a bit with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a window, so let's use it. Get the agreements signed, get the training funded, get a plan for the town. I'd say that in the crib room and at the union meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is long enough for me to do my usual thing: wait for someone to try something, then follow. I'd probably follow people into surface control jobs, then maybe into something like mine rehab, filling in the old pits and replanting. But that's me guessing, I honestly don't know what's left at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd keep my job, push savings to six months, and do a short course in mine closure and rehabilitation at the technical college at night. I'd watch which of the older guys move first and talk to them. And I'd stay on the union committee to push for a training fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the useful kind. The kind that gets you to sign up for things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why mine rehab?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because someone has to fix the holes we made, and it takes years, and the law says it has to be done. I grew up next to an old tin pit that was just left, orange water and dead trees. It would feel decent to be on that side of it for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the extra time change how you feel about your mum and the money you send?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. With five years I could tell her straight, I'll keep helping for three more, then we work out something else with my brother. That's a real conversation. With two years there's nothing to plan, just bad news.

S3.say: We've got a window, so let's use it: sign the agreements, fund the training, make a plan for the town. I'd say it in the crib room and at union meetings.
S3.think: Five years is long enough for me to do my usual thing, wait for someone to try something and then follow. Maybe surface control, then mine rehabilitation, but I honestly don't know what's left at the end.
S3.do: Keeps her job, pushes savings to six months, and takes a night course in mine closure and rehabilitation at the technical college. Watches which older colleagues move first and stays on the union committee pushing for a training fund.
S3.feel: Anxious, but the useful kind that gets her to sign up for things.
S3.quote: Someone has to fix the holes we made, and it takes years, and the law says it has to be done.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Grace enough room to use her follow-second style again, which visibly relaxed her. Mine rehabilitation links to a childhood memory of an abandoned tin pit. She's honest that she doesn't know what work remains at the end point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a whole career, almost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if we're serious, so no excuses this time. Governments, companies, unions, everyone gets a job to do. Online I'd say it a bit more politely than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years makes me think I'd be okay for most of it. I could get to surface control, then rehab, then whatever comes after. The end point still scares me, but it's far enough away that it feels like weather, not like a fire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the drill for now and watch the remote trials closely. In the first year I'd start the rehab course part-time and maybe sit the surface control ticket once it exists. Me and my sister would talk about buying a small place together, to stop renting, maybe in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but the kind you can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said weather, not fire. What's the difference for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Weather, you look at the sky, you take a coat, you change your plans a bit. Fire, you grab what you can and run. Ten years is weather. Two years is fire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do with ten years that you wouldn't with two or five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buy something with my sister, maybe. And actually think about kids one day, which I'd put off forever in the two-year picture. Ten years is enough time to have a life in it, not just a plan.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty if we're serious, so no excuses this time. Governments, companies and unions all get a job to do.
S4.think: I think I'd be okay for most of the ten years, moving from the drill to surface control to rehab. The end point still scares me, but it feels like weather, not a fire.
S4.do: Keeps drilling while watching the remote trials, starts the rehabilitation course part-time, and plans to sit a surface control ticket when one exists. Talks with her sister about buying a small place together within five years.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but in a way she feels she can work with.
S4.quote: Ten years is weather. Two years is fire.
S4.fieldNote: Grace's feelings track the warning time very closely: fire for two years, weather for ten. With a decade she starts to picture a life, buying with her sister and maybe children, not just a survival plan. She still names the end point as frightening.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two years, without a doubt. It takes away the only way I know to deal with change, which is let someone else try it first. What would help is a wage floor that comes in straight away, paid for by the companies that save the money, and free courses at night that don't make you choose between rent and learning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked about women in mining. It took me six years to get to lead hand. If the remote jobs get handed out by who plays golf with the manager, women will be the last ones moved up, again. I'd want those jobs given out fairly, by skill.

headlineQuote: I'd be checking the job boards in the toilet at break.
portrait: Grace Okafor is 27, single, and leads a development drilling crew nine hundred metres underground at a gold mine. She's careful and methodical, uses AI now and then for paperwork, and likes to go second with any new technology, once others have ironed out the bugs. She sends part of her pay to her mother and has about three months saved. Through the scenarios she leans on the union and on government, worries most about older colleagues, and finds that her follow-second approach only works when there's time. With ten years she starts to imagine a real life, not just a plan.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it removes her way of coping with change: letting someone else try it first.
whatWouldHelp: A wage floor that starts straight away, paid for by the companies that save the money, and free night courses that don't force a choice between rent and learning.
